337.title: Bo: a sign upon your hand (Exodus 13:9, 16)
337.hook: the Exodus is remembered on the hand and between the eyes, a root of tefillin
337.howItsDone: Many Jews, traditionally men and in some communities women too, put on tefillin for weekday morning prayer, binding one box on the arm and one on the head; tefillin are not worn on Shabbat or festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, haggadah, the telling. Your line was tell your child. Which story did you pass on? Today, the last day of Bo, and a memory you wear instead of tell. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

A wedding ring. A string on a wrist from a grandmother. A watch that belonged to someone who's gone. A medical bracelet. Some things we remember in our heads, and some we remember on our skin, where our hands brush them a hundred times a day without our trying. Bo is ending. The plagues are over, the night of the Exodus has come and gone, and the people are finally out. And the portion's last word on the matter isn't a story or a song. It's a sign, worn on the body.
screen: `A RING. A STRING. A WATCH.` → `MEMORY ON THE SKIN.` → `BO ENDS WITH A SIGN.`

segments.voice: Twice, near the end of Bo, the Torah says the Exodus should be remembered on the body. The first time: "And it shall be for a sign unto thee upon thy hand, and for a memorial between thine eyes." The second time, a few verses later, it's for a sign upon thy hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes. Jewish tradition reads these verses, and two more in Deuteronomy, as the command of tefillin: two small black leather boxes, one bound on the arm facing the heart, one on the head above the forehead, worn by many Jews for weekday morning prayer. Here's the thing to know. Inside the boxes are four handwritten passages from the Torah. Two of them are from this very portion, the two we just heard. The other two are from Deuteronomy, the Shema and the paragraph after it. So every morning the Exodus is literally strapped on. The word for frontlets, totafot, is a puzzle; nobody is certain where it comes from. The Talmud plays with it as two foreign words that each mean two, which add up to the four compartments of the head box. Whatever its origin, the idea is plain: memory that lives only in your head fades. Memory bound to your hand and your eyes stays where you'll keep bumping into it. And with that, Bo is done: come, not go; the darkness; the new moon; the telling; and the sign on the hand.
screen: `A SIGN UPON THY HAND.` · `FOUR PASSAGES, TWO FROM BO.` · `TOTAFOT: A PUZZLE WORD.` · `MEMORY BOUND TO THE BODY.` · then, large: `REMEMBER WITH YOUR BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the reminder on you. Settle, and breathe. Rest one hand on your other forearm. Feel the weight of it. Is there anything you wear that carries a memory? A ring, a bracelet, a scar you've made peace with, even a shirt someone gave you. If there is, touch it and let the memory come. If not, choose something now, a ring, a hair tie, a watch on the other wrist, and give it a job: to remind you of one thing you've been freed from. The bell holds the time.
Bo. Come. The portion we finish today, which ends by binding the Exodus to the hand and between the eyes.
Your line: remember with your body. Today, wear that reminder, and each time you notice it, remember what it's for. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

338.title: Beshalach: the long way round (Exodus 13:17)
338.hook: God leads them away from the short road lest they see war and turn back
338.carry: the long way can be kinder
338.howItsDone: Beshalach is read in synagogue in winter, on the Shabbat called Shabbat Shirah, the Sabbath of song, because it contains the Song at the Sea, which the congregation often stands for.

segments.voice: Yesterday Bo ended with a sign upon the hand. Your line was remember with your body. Did you wear your reminder? Today, a new portion, and the people's first steps out. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

Open a map app and it hands you the fastest route, down to the minute. It doesn't know you hate that interchange. It doesn't know you've only just learned to drive, or that the quick road runs past the house of someone you can't face yet. Sometimes the shortest road is the one most likely to make you turn around. The Israelites are free. They're standing at the edge of Egypt, and the quickest road to the promised land runs straight along the coast. A new portion begins here, and the very first thing it tells us is that God doesn't take it.
screen: `THE FASTEST ROUTE.` → `THE ROAD THAT MAKES YOU TURN BACK.` → `GOD DOESN'T TAKE IT.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Beshalach, from its first phrase: when Pharaoh had let the people go. The short way, the verse says, was the way of the land of the Philistines, along the sea. It was near. And God led them another way, and the Torah gives the reason in God's own words: "Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt." Repent here means change their minds. People who had been slaves the day before weren't ready for a battle. One look at an army and Egypt would have seemed safe again. So God sends them the long way, through the wilderness, toward the sea. It's the first route decision of the free people, and it's made for their sake, not for speed. Maimonides, the great twelfth-century philosopher, leaned on this verse. He said it shows how God works with human nature rather than against it. People can't leap from one way of life to its opposite overnight. So the Torah leads them gently, step by step, the way you'd lead someone who's frightened. He even used the verse to explain why the long years in the wilderness were needed, to raise a generation used to freedom. Notice what the long way isn't. It isn't avoidance. The sea is still coming, and so are hard days. It's a road sized to who you are right now, so you don't give up before you arrive.
screen: `BESHALACH: WHEN HE LET GO.` · `THE SHORT ROAD: PHILISTINE LAND.` · `LEST THEY SEE WAR AND TURN BACK.` · `MAIMONIDES: STEP BY STEP.` · then, large: `THE LONG WAY CAN BE KINDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at your route. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're trying to change, a habit, a relationship, a part of yourself. Have you been taking the shortest road, all at once, and turning back every time it gets hard? Picture a longer road instead. A smaller first step. A slower pace that you could actually keep. Don't decide everything. Just see the longer road, and notice whether it feels kinder. The bell holds the time.
Beshalach. When he let go. The portion of the sea, which opens with God choosing the long road so a frightened people won't turn back.
Your line: the long way can be kinder. Today, take the longer road once: the slower walk, the gentler start, the extra explanation. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

339.title: Beshalach: Joseph's bones (Exodus 13:19)
339.hook: while others gather silver, Moses carries Joseph's bones, keeping an old promise
339.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats keeping one's word as weighty, and promises to the dying especially so; Moses carrying Joseph's bones is often taught as the model of a promise kept across generations.

segments.voice: Yesterday God chose the road along the wilderness, not the short one. Your line was the long way can be kinder. Did you take a longer road once? Today, what Moses carries on it. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

Picture moving day after a hundred years in the same house. Everyone is grabbing what matters to them: the good dishes, the jewelry, the papers. And one person is up in the attic, looking for something nobody else remembers. A promise someone made, long before any of them were born. The Israelites are leaving Egypt in a hurry, and the Torah stops, in the middle of the march, for one short verse about what Moses chose to pack.
screen: `MOVING DAY, A HUNDRED YEARS ON.` → `EVERYONE GRABS WHAT MATTERS.` → `ONE PERSON IN THE ATTIC.`

segments.voice: "And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him." That's the verse. To hear why it matters, go back to the very end of Genesis. Joseph, dying in Egypt, made his brothers swear: when God remembers you and brings you out of here, carry my bones up with you. Generations passed. Slavery came. Most people must have forgotten. Moses didn't. The Talmud, in a well-known passage, sets a scene around that verse. On the night of leaving, it says, the Israelites were busy with the silver and gold the Egyptians had given them. The Torah does tell us they asked for and received jewels of silver and gold. But Moses, the Talmud says, was busy with Joseph's bones. And it quotes a line from Proverbs about Moses: the wise in heart takes on commandments. Everyone else carried treasure. He carried a promise. The rabbis tell more: that Joseph's coffin had been sunk in the Nile, and an old woman named Serach, Joseph's niece, was the one who remembered where. That part is midrash, a story the tradition tells, not the plain text. The plain text does finish the arc, though, much later. In the book of Joshua, Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem, in the land. A promise made by brothers, kept by a descendant of one of those brothers, finished by a generation not yet born. The Hebrew word for bone, etzem, also means essence, the self. Moses carried Joseph's very self out of Egypt.
screen: `AND MOSES TOOK THE BONES.` · `JOSEPH'S OATH, END OF GENESIS.` · `SILVER FOR THEM, BONES FOR MOSES.` · `BURIED AT SHECHEM, AT LAST.` · then, large: `CARRY THE BONES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find an old promise. Settle, and breathe. Think back. Is there something you said you'd do, maybe years ago, maybe to someone who's no longer around? Call your aunt. Finish the photo album. Visit the town your grandfather came from. Learn the recipe. Let one promise come up, even a small one. Don't judge yourself for how long it's waited. Joseph's waited a long time too. Just hold it, and ask: what's one step that would carry it a little further? The bell holds the time.
Beshalach. When he let go. Our portion, where Moses leaves Egypt carrying Joseph's bones, an old promise kept.
Your line: carry the bones. Today, take one real step on an old promise, even just writing it down where you'll see it. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

340.title: Beshalach: stop praying, move (Exodus 14:15)
340.hook: at the sea, God asks Moses why he cries out, and tells the people to go forward
340.howItsDone: The crossing of the sea is read in synagogue twice a year: in the weekly portion Beshalach, and on the seventh day of Passover, which tradition dates to the night of the crossing. Nachshon is often taught to children as the one who stepped in first.

segments.voice: Yesterday Moses packed Joseph's bones while everyone else packed silver. Your line was carry the bones. Did you take a step on an old promise? Today, the sea in front of them, and an army behind. Day three hundred forty.

Everyone has stood at a fork like this. The email you keep drafting and not sending. The doctor's appointment you keep meaning to book. You've thought about it, worried about it, maybe prayed about it, and at some point the thinking has become a place to hide. The Israelites are trapped. The sea is in front of them, and Pharaoh's chariots are coming up behind. The people cry out in terror. Moses tells them to stand still and watch. And then God says something to Moses that sounds, at first, almost like a rebuke.
screen: `THE EMAIL YOU NEVER SEND.` → `SEA IN FRONT, CHARIOTS BEHIND.` → `GOD SPEAKS TO MOSES.`

segments.voice: God asks Moses why he is crying out. Then: "speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward." Here's the strange part. The Torah never shows Moses crying out. The people cried out, a few verses earlier. Moses told them to be calm. So what is God answering? Rashi, the medieval commentator, says the verse teaches that Moses was standing and praying, silently, and God's reply means: this is not the time for long prayer. Israel is in danger. Move. It isn't that prayer is wrong. Moses prayed many times, and God listened. It's that prayer has a time, and so does walking. The rabbis then tell a famous story about who took the first step. In the Talmud, Rabbi Judah says the tribes stood at the shore, each wanting someone else to go first. Then Nachshon, son of Amminadav, of the tribe of Judah, jumped into the water. In some tellings, he waded in until it reached his neck, and only then did the sea split. That's midrash, a story the tradition tells about the gap between one verse and the next. The Torah itself simply says Moses lifted his rod, stretched his hand over the sea, and a strong east wind blew all night. But the story has stuck because it names something true. Sometimes the sea parts in front of people who are already walking.
screen: `WHY DO YOU CRY OUT TO ME?` · `RASHI: NOT THE TIME FOR LONG PRAYER.` · `NACHSHON STEPS IN FIRST.` · `THE STRONG EAST WIND.` · then, large: `PRAY, THEN GO FORWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the sea in front of you. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been circling. You've thought about it enough. If you pray, pray about it now, briefly and honestly. If you don't, just name it clearly to yourself. Then picture the very first step. Not the whole crossing. One step: the first sentence of the email, the phone number dialed, the shoes put on. See your foot touching the water. The bell holds the time.
Beshalach. When he let go. Our portion, where at the edge of the sea God tells Moses: speak to the people, and let them go forward.
Your line: pray, then go forward. Today, take the first step on the thing you've been circling, right after you finish thinking about it. Day three hundred forty.

341.title: Beshalach: bitter water made sweet (Exodus 15:22–26)
341.hook: at Marah the water is bitter until a tree is thrown in
341.howItsDone: The Song at the Sea, sung just before the Marah story, is part of the daily morning service, and the words 'I am the LORD that heals you' are often quoted in Jewish prayers and blessings for healing.

segments.voice: Yesterday the people stood at the sea and God said go forward. Your line was pray, then go forward. Did you take a first step? Today, still in Beshalach, they're across, and three days later, thirsty. Day three hundred forty-one.

Big wins have a strange aftertaste. The wedding is over and now there are thank-you notes. The new job starts and the commute is awful. The graduation party ends and the loans begin. The Israelites have just walked through the sea on dry land. They've sung a song that Jews still sing every morning. And three days later, in the wilderness of Shur, they still haven't found water. When they finally do, at a place called Marah, they lift it to their lips and spit it out.
screen: `THE WIN, THEN THE AFTERTASTE.` → `THREE DAYS, NO WATER.` → `MARAH: THEY SPIT IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Marah means bitter. The place is named for the water, and the people do what thirsty people do: they complain to Moses. What shall we drink? Moses cries out to God, and God shows him a tree, a piece of wood. Moses throws it into the water, and in the old Jewish translation, "the waters were made sweet." That's it. A few verses. The Torah doesn't say what kind of tree it was, and the rabbis couldn't resist asking. In the Mekhilta, an early commentary, several sages each name a different tree. One opinion is that it was itself bitter, and the lesson is that God can heal bitter with bitter. Another says the tree was a symbol for the words of Torah, which the book of Proverbs calls a tree of life. And then the story ends with a line people have carried far beyond the wilderness: "for I am the LORD that healeth thee." Notice what the story doesn't do. It doesn't scold them for being thirsty. It doesn't take them back to the sea. The bitterness is real, and something is thrown into the middle of it, and it changes. Sometimes the change is a tree in the water: a meal someone brings, a joke at the right moment, an old song, a page of something wise. Small things, dropped into the bitter part.
screen: `MARAH: BITTER.` · `A TREE THROWN IN, MADE SWEET.` · `WHICH TREE? THE SAGES DISAGREE.` · `THE LORD THAT HEALETH THEE.` · then, large: `A TREE IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the bitter water. Settle, and breathe. Think of one bitter thing in your life right now. Not the biggest one. A smaller one: a tense email thread, a chore you hate, a sour mood between you and someone. Taste it honestly. Then ask: what's one small thing I could throw into it? A kind word, a cup of tea, a walk, a sentence of thanks, a song. Picture dropping it in. If you pray, you can hold the line from Marah, the LORD that healeth thee. The bell holds the time.
Beshalach. When he let go. Our portion, where just past the sea the water turns bitter, and a tree thrown in makes it sweet.
Your line: a tree in the water. Today, when something tastes bitter, look for one small thing to drop into it. Day three hundred forty-one.

342.title: Beshalach: held-up hands (Exodus 17:8–13)
342.hook: when Moses' arms tire, Aaron and Hur hold them up until sunset
342.howItsDone: The Amalek story is read in synagogue on the morning of Purim, since Haman is traditionally linked to Amalek, and on the Shabbat before Purim the command to remember Amalek is read from Deuteronomy.

segments.voice: Yesterday at Marah, bitter water turned sweet. Your line was a tree in the water. What did you drop into something bitter? Today, the last day of Beshalach, and a battle. Day three hundred forty-two.

Try holding your arms straight out in front of you. Not for a few seconds. For a minute. Then five. Then imagine an afternoon. The shoulders burn first, then the forearms shake, and at some point your arms just drop, no matter how much you care. The Israelites are camped at a place called Rephidim when a people called Amalek attacks them. Joshua leads the fighters below. Moses climbs a hill with the staff of God in his hand. And the battle comes down to something as ordinary and human as tired arms.
screen: `ARMS OUT FOR A MINUTE.` → `THEN AN AFTERNOON.` → `AMALEK ATTACKS.`

segments.voice: When Moses holds up his hands, Israel prevails. When he lets them down, Amalek prevails. And his hands get heavy. So two people step in. Aaron, his brother, and Hur, a man we barely meet anywhere else. They put a stone under Moses so he can sit, and they stand on either side holding up his arms, one on each side, "and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun." The word for steady, emunah, is the word usually translated faith. His hands were faithfulness, held up by friends. The Mishnah asks the obvious question. Did Moses' hands win or lose a war? No, it says. When Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to their Father in heaven, they prevailed, and when they didn't, they fell. The hands were a sign pointing up. The Talmud notices the stone. Why not a cushion? Because Moses wouldn't sit in comfort while his people were suffering in the fight. And Amalek itself becomes a name in Jewish memory. Deuteronomy says they struck at the weary and the stragglers at the rear. In tradition, Amalek comes to stand for cruelty that targets the weak. So Beshalach ends where it began, with a people learning to walk: the long way round, Joseph's bones, the sea, bitter water, and now, Moses on a hill, held up by friends.
screen: `HANDS UP, ISRAEL PREVAILS.` · `AARON AND HUR, ONE ON EACH SIDE.` · `MISHNAH: HEARTS LOOKING UPWARD.` · `A STONE, NOT A CUSHION.` · then, large: `HOLD UP THE HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the tired arms. Settle, and breathe. If you can, lift your arms a little in front of you and feel how soon they want to fall. Then rest them. Now think of who in your life is holding something up all day: a parent caring for a child or an aging mother, a teacher, a nurse, a friend carrying a cause. Picture standing beside them like Aaron, or like Hur. What would holding up their arms look like this week? The bell holds the time.
Amalek. The people who attacked Israel at Rephidim, striking at the weary, and the battle won while friends held up Moses' tired hands.
Your line: hold up the hands. Today, find one tired person and take some of the weight: a meal, a ride, an hour, a message that says I see how much you carry. Day three hundred forty-two.

343.title: Yitro: named for an outsider
343.hook: the portion with the Ten Words is named for Jethro, a Midianite priest
343.howItsDone: Yitro is read in synagogue in winter; when the Ten Commandments are chanted, many congregations stand. Jewish teachers often point out that the portion is named for Jethro, a Midianite priest.

segments.voice: Yesterday Amalek attacked, and Aaron and Hur held up Moses' tired arms. Your line was hold up the hands. Whose weight did you share? Today, a new portion, and a visitor. Day three hundred forty-three.

Here's a question for a trivia night. Which portion of the Torah contains the Ten Commandments, the moment at Mount Sinai, thunder, smoke, the voice of God? And what's that portion called? Not Moses. Not Sinai. Not the Ten Words. It's named after Moses' father-in-law, a priest of Midian, who wasn't an Israelite at all. His name was Jethro. In Hebrew, Yitro. And before Sinai even comes into view, he walks into the camp and tells Moses he's doing his job wrong.
screen: `WHERE ARE THE TEN COMMANDMENTS?` → `NAMED FOR A PRIEST OF MIDIAN.` → `YITRO WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: Yitro has heard everything God did for Israel, and he comes to the wilderness bringing Moses' wife Zipporah and their two sons. Moses tells him the whole story. And Yitro rejoices, and blesses the God who rescued them. The next morning he watches Moses sit as judge for the people, from morning until evening, everyone lining up with their disputes. And he says, in the old Jewish translation: "The thing that thou doest is not good." You'll wear yourself out, and the people too. Then he offers a plan. Find capable, honest, God-fearing people. Make them judges over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Let them handle the small cases and bring you the great ones. And here's the remarkable part: Moses listens. He does what his father-in-law says. The first court system of Israel, in the Torah's telling, comes from the advice of an outsider. Rashi, quoting the old midrash, says Yitro had seven names, and one of them, Yeter, means addition, because he added a section to the Torah. The rabbis even argued about the timing: did he come before Sinai, or after, and the Torah moved his story here? They didn't settle it. But there it sits, right before the Ten Words, and the portion carries his name. A tradition that names its holiest week of reading after a Midianite priest is saying something about where wisdom can come from.
